s.x: **Purpose:** To recount the establishment of the Israelite monarchy and to highlight the differing character of Israel’s first two kings
**Date:** Records events that occurred around 1050–1011 BC
**Setting:** The transition from the period of the judges to the Israelite monarchy

i.x: The right leadership can give people a sense of safety when neighboring nations are hostile. In Samuel’s time, Israel faced external threats and internal discord, and the judges only provided a fleeting sense of security. Israel wanted a king. The book of 1 Samuel records Israel’s transition from a federation of tribes to a centralized kingdom. Saul, Israel’s first king, did not remain faithful to God. But then God chose David as king, and God’s plan to save Israel—and the world—began to unfold.
Setting

Moses had predicted that the people of Israel would ask for a king to reign over them ([Deut 17:14-20](Deut.17.14-Deut.17.20)). God spelled out the requirements for a king ([Deut 17:15](Deut.17.15)) but also warned of the evils commonly associated with human kings. A king would want many horses, numerous wives, and large sums of gold and silver ([Deut 17:16-17](Deut.17.16-Deut.17.17)). To mitigate these tendencies, God instructed that each king of Israel must study God’s law ([Deut 17:18-20](Deut.17.18-Deut.17.20)).

Throughout the days of the judges, Israel’s tribes lacked unity (see [Judg 17–21](Judg.17.1-Judg.21.25)). By Samuel’s time, Israel was looking for a king to unite the nation and protect it from internal and external threats.

Gideon, who judged Israel about one hundred years before the time of Samuel, had acted a lot like a king. Gideon rejected the invitation to inaugurate a hereditary dynasty ([Judg 8:22-23](Judg.8.22-Judg.8.23)), but he began to act like a king: He accumulated gold and used it to build a religious idol ([Judg 8:24-27](Judg.8.24-Judg.8.27)), he took many wives ([Judg 8:30](Judg.8.30)), and he even named one of his sons Abimelech, which means “my father is king” ([Judg 8:31](Judg.8.31)). Gideon acted like the kind of king God wanted Israel never to have. A monarchy would give an imperfect human even more control than the judges exercised. 1 Samuel records the trouble that surrounded Israel’s first king, Saul, and begins to outline God’s unfolding plan to establish an eternal kingship through the line of David.
Summary

In [1 Samuel 1–7](1Sam.1.1-1Sam.7.17), Samuel emerges as a judge and prophet of God. Samuel was born to a devout woman named Hannah, who had previously been barren ([1:1-23](1Sam.1.1-1Sam.1.23)). As a young child, Samuel, a Levite, ([1 Chr 6:33-34](1Chr.6.33-1Chr.6.34)) became an apprentice in the Tabernacle under the supervision of Eli the priest ([1:24–3:18](1Sam.1.24-1Sam.3.18)). Likely trained to be a Tabernacle assistant, Samuel instead became a prophet with a growing reputation ([3:19–4:1](1Sam.3.19-1Sam.4.1)a). Evidently, he was not yet prominent in Israel’s national life when the Philistines harassed the Israelites and captured the Ark of the Covenant ([4:1–7:2](1Sam.4.1-1Sam.7.2)), as he is absent from that narrative. In chapter [7](1Sam.7.1-1Sam.7.17), Samuel reappears, calling Israel to repentance; and acting as a judge, he drove out the Philistine oppressors.

Samuel’s leadership as Levite, prophet, and judge spanned all spheres of public life. Yet his sons did not prove worthy of carrying on in his place ([8:1-3](1Sam.8.1-1Sam.8.3)), so Israel asked Samuel to appoint a king to lead them, just like the other nations. Samuel was outspoken in his opposition ([8:10-21](1Sam.8.10-1Sam.8.21)), yet the Lord instructed Samuel to anoint Saul as king (chs [9–10](1Sam.9.1-1Sam.10.27)). In his farewell address, Samuel reminded the Israelites of God’s power and care for them (ch [12](1Sam.12.1-1Sam.12.25)). He wanted them to realize their sin in asking for a king rather than trusting in the Lord.

Initially, Saul was a good king. He defeated the neighboring Ammonites and saved the city of Jabesh-gilead from doom (ch [11](1Sam.11.1-1Sam.11.15)). But Saul soon proved, by his disobedience to God, that he was unworthy to be Israel’s king (chs [13](1Sam.13.1-1Sam.13.23), [15](1Sam.15.1-1Sam.15.35)). By contrast, Saul’s noble son Jonathan seemed to be an ideal successor ([14:1-52](1Sam.14.1-1Sam.14.52)). But Jonathan would not succeed Saul, because God had different plans (chs [16–31](1Sam.16.1-1Sam.31.13)). God instructed Samuel to anoint David secretly as Saul’s successor while Saul was still king ([16:1-13](1Sam.16.1-1Sam.16.13)).

Saul’s relationship with David was good at first, thanks in part to David’s musical gifts ([16:14-23](1Sam.16.14-1Sam.16.23)). However, David’s success with Goliath ([17:1-58](1Sam.17.1-1Sam.17.58)) made Saul jealous ([18:6-16](1Sam.18.6-1Sam.18.16)), and Saul tried to eliminate the threat David posed to his kingship. He brought David into his family by marriage to provide greater opportunities to kill him ([18:17-29](1Sam.18.17-1Sam.18.29)). He attacked David directly ([19:1-10](1Sam.19.1-1Sam.19.10)) and executed anybody who harbored David (chs [21–22](1Sam.21.1-1Sam.22.23)). Yet all of Saul’s attempts to eliminate David proved unsuccessful.

Both Saul and Jonathan died in battle against the Philistines ([31:1-6](1Sam.31.1-1Sam.31.6)). This paved the way for David to begin his reign, though not without further difficulties (see [2 Sam 1:1–5:5](2Sam.1.1-2Sam.5.5)).
Authorship

The title “Samuel” comes from the important role Samuel played in Israel’s transition to a monarchy, not from the book’s authorship. Samuel could have written parts of 1 Samuel, but he could not have written any part of 2 Samuel, as his death is recorded in [1 Samuel 25:1](1Sam.25.1). The final editor of 1 Samuel is never identified.
Composition

The books of 1–2 Samuel were originally one book. The translators of the Septuagint (the Greek Old Testament) divided it into two books, 1–2 Kingdoms. Later Hebrew tradition also divided the book but retained the name Samuel, as do most English versions.

Some scholars contend that 1–2 Samuel (along with 1–2 Kings, also one book originally) were created from a variety of sources during or after the Babylonian Exile (586–538 BC). Multiple sources were doubtless used in 1–2 Samuel—for example, Samuel, Nathan, and Gad all chronicled events from the life of David ([1 Chronicles 29:29](1Chr.29.29)). The inspired author of 1–2 Samuel would have made use of such information. However, the book also could have been near its final form during or shortly after the reign of Solomon (971–931 BC).

Shortly after Judah’s exile to Babylon, 1–2 Samuel was incorporated into the larger body of material that also includes Joshua, Judges, and 1–2 Kings. This section of Scripture traces Israel’s sacred history, beginning with blessing (conquering the land) and ending with judgment (losing the land). It explains to an audience in exile how their grave misfortune came about.
Manuscripts

The text of 1–2 Samuel that is found in the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint, 200s BC) is different in many places from the Hebrew (Masoretic) text (around AD 1000). The Hebrew texts of Samuel in the Dead Sea Scrolls (around 250–50 BC) found at Qumran agree in some places with the Septuagint, in other places with the Masoretic Text. In still other places the Dead Sea texts have their own readings. Readers will encounter notes such as “Hebrew lacks . . . ” or “Greek reads . . . ” more frequently in 1–2 Samuel than in other Old Testament books. However, few of these textual variants significantly alter the meaning.
Meaning and Message

The emphasis on kingship in 1 Samuel first appears in Hannah’s prayer (see [2:10](1Sam.2.10)). The idea that Israel would have a king was as old as God’s promise to Abraham and Sarah ([Gen 17:6](Gen.17.6), [16](Gen.17.16)). God neither mandated nor forbade a monarchy but only spelled out the excesses from which Israel’s kings must abstain (see [Deut 17:14-20](Deut.17.14-Deut.17.20)).

During the period of the judges, Israel changed dramatically for the worse—both spiritually and nationally. This steady disintegration reaches a horrible climax in [Judges 17–21](Judg.17.1-Judg.21.25). The book of Judges hints that, to help correct this decline, Israel needed a king. Israel’s greatest threat was not the Philistines or any other predatory neighbor but Israel itself and its breaking of the covenant. Israel needed a king to guard the covenant, which the pre-monarchical order had put at risk.

If the king’s responsibility was to administer the covenant ([Deut 17:18-20](Deut.17.18-Deut.17.20)), the prophet’s duty was to interpret its stipulations. For this reason, the prophet Samuel protected his divinely authorized claim over kings with a holy zeal. Not only did Samuel anoint Israel’s first two kings ([1 Sam 10:1](1Sam.10.1); [16:13](1Sam.16.13)), but he was also compelled to censure the king when he stepped outside of covenantal boundaries ([13:8-15](1Sam.13.8-1Sam.13.15); [15:10-33](1Sam.15.10-1Sam.15.33)).

Saul did not have the character or integrity needed to lead Israel into a successful, God-honoring monarchy. Saul was not fated to fall, as though he had no control over his decisions. In fact, God wanted him to be a good king and made every provision for that to happen (such as changing his heart and giving him his Spirit). But God does not force righteousness, holiness, or obedience. His grace is persuasive but not coercive.

Despite the deep disappointments of the era of the judges and the early monarchy, God’s sovereign control over Israel’s history is demonstrated in several ways: (1) A once-barren woman gave birth to Samuel, God’s agent for the transition to monarchy (ch [1](1Sam.1.1-1Sam.1.28)); (2) a devastating Philistine victory became a Philistine defeat without human participation (chs [4–6](1Sam.4.1-1Sam.6.21)); (3) the king whom the people demanded became God’s anointed (chs [8–10](1Sam.8.1-1Sam.10.27)); (4) this king was rejected by God for his unfaithfulness (chs [13](1Sam.13.1-1Sam.13.23), [15](1Sam.15.1-1Sam.15.35)); and (5) the eighth son of an obscure family, a man after God’s own heart, was chosen as the future king of Israel (ch [16](1Sam.16.1-1Sam.16.23)).

Unlike Saul’s rule, David’s kingship over Israel lasted, and one of his descendants later became the sovereign King of the whole world. Jesus is the final heir to David’s throne ([John 7:42](John.7.42); [Rev 5:5](Rev.5.5); [11:15](Rev.11.15)). He perpetuates his ancestor’s virtues but never exhibits his flaws. Jesus is the world’s perfect and eternal Shepherd and King.

b.x: **Elkanah** was a Levite ([1 Chr 6:22-27](1Chr.6.22-1Chr.6.27)). After the conquest of the Promised Land, the Levites were given towns in the territories of the other Israelite tribes, including **Ephraim** ([Josh 21:20](Josh.21.20)).

Elkanah’s hometown was **Ramah** ([1 Sam 2:11](1Sam.2.11)). This location should not be confused with the Ramah in the tribal area of Benjamin (see [Josh 18:25](Josh.18.25); [Judg 19:13](Judg.19.13); [Matt 2:18](Matt.2.18)).

The **region of Zuph** was named after one of Elkanah’s ancestors, a Levite of the clan of Kohath ([1 Chr 6:35](1Chr.6.35)). Saul first met Samuel in Zuph while searching for his father’s donkeys ([1 Sam 9:5](1Sam.9.5)).
Elkanah’s lengthy genealogy suggests he was socially prominent.

Hardly an instance exists in Scripture where a man’s simultaneous marriage to **two wives** did not produce serious friction ([1:6-7](1Sam.1.6-1Sam.1.7); [Gen 16](Gen.16.1-Gen.16.16); [21](Gen.21.1-Gen.21.34); [29](Gen.29.1-Gen.29.35)).
Elkanah made this trip **each year***;* the law required that people attend three annual festivals ([Exod 23:14-17](Exod.23.14-Exod.23.17)).

According to God’s law, Israelites were to **sacrifice** at God’s chosen sanctuary ([Deut 12:1-28](Deut.12.1-Deut.12.28)). From the days of Joshua ([Josh 18:1](Josh.18.1)) through Samuel’s era, God’s sanctuary—the Tabernacle—was at **Shiloh***,* a town in Ephraim some 8.5 miles north of Bethel en route to Shechem. King David eventually moved it to Jerusalem ([2 Sam 6](2Sam.6.1-2Sam.6.23)).

**the** **LORD of Heaven’s Armies:** Throughout the Hebrew Old Testament, God is often referred to as *Yahweh Tseba’oth* or *’Elohim Tseba’oth*. Traditionally, these titles have been translated “LORD of hosts” and “God of hosts.” The term “hosts” (Hebrew *tseba’oth,* traditionally “sabaoth”) usually means “armies.” It can refer to human armies, such as the armies of Israel (e.g., [1 Sam 17:45](1Sam.17.45)), or foreign armies sent to fulfill the Lord’s purposes (e.g., [Isa 9:11-13](Isa.9.11-Isa.9.13)). However, most often it refers to God’s angelic armies sent from heaven to do his bidding and wage war on earth (e.g., [2 Kgs 6:17](2Kgs.6.17)). This designation anticipates God’s role as a mighty warrior in the episode involving the Ark of the Covenant and the Philistines ([1 Sam 4–6](1Sam.4.1-1Sam.6.21)).
**sacrifice . . . portions of the meat:** Certain sacrifices involved sharing part of the sacrificial animal in a communal meal (see [Lev 7:11-34](Lev.7.11-Lev.7.34)).
**the Tabernacle:** Also called “the Temple of the LORD” in [1:9](1Sam.1.9). These designations reflect that the Tabernacle, a portable structure, served as the central sanctuary at Shiloh.
**the Tabernacle:** Literally *the Temple of the* *LORD*. Solomon’s Temple had not yet been constructed, so the word *Temple* here means the Lord’s sanctuary.

Hannah’s **vow** was a promise to give the child back to the Lord as a Nazirite (see [Num 6:1-21](Num.6.1-Num.6.21)). Hannah might have hoped that her child would be another Samson (cp. [Judg 13](Judg.13.1-Judg.13.25)), a deliverer of God’s people.

Some people might have used the feast times at Shiloh as an occasion to get **drunk** rather than to worship. Eli mistakenly assumed Hannah was another drunken reveler (cp. [Acts 2:13-15](Acts.2.13-Acts.2.15)).

**wicked woman** (Hebrew *a daughter of Belial*): An expression used to describe a worthless person. Belial (“worthlessness”) is later used as a name for Satan ([2 Cor 6:15](2Cor.6.15)). In Hebrew, a *son of* or *daughter of* a quality is a person who exemplifies that quality.

A blessing was more than mere wishful thinking. It was often God’s means of conferring a real benefit (see, e.g., [Gen 27:1-40](Gen.27.1-Gen.27.40); [28:1-4](Gen.28.1-Gen.28.4); [32:22-32](Gen.32.22-Gen.32.32); [48:1–49:28](Gen.48.1-Gen.49.28)). Because this blessing from God’s high priest provided assurance that Hannah’s prayer would be answered, she was **no longer sad**.
**until the boy is weaned:** Hannah would have nursed Samuel two to four years.
Elkanah could have overridden Hannah’s **promise** ([Num 30:12-14](Num.30.12-Num.30.14)), but instead he affirmed and supported it.

Hannah’s Prayer of Praise celebrates Samuel’s dedication to the Lord’s service by rejoicing in God’s uniqueness ([2:1-2](1Sam.2.1-1Sam.2.2)), his ability to reverse fortunes ([2:3-9](1Sam.2.3-1Sam.2.9)), and his ability to strengthen his chosen king ([2:10](1Sam.2.10)). Like Mary’s Song of Praise ([Luke 1:46-55](Luke.1.46-Luke.1.55)), Hannah’s prayer emphasizes God bringing down the rich and powerful and exalting the poor and the downtrodden ([1 Sam 2:7-8](1Sam.2.7-1Sam.2.8); [Luke 1:52-53](Luke.1.52-Luke.1.53)). David’s prayer in [2 Sam 22](2Sam.22.1-2Sam.22.51) is another beautiful proclamation of God’s saving power as it relates to his chosen king ([1 Sam 2:10](1Sam.2.10)). The rich, unrighteous rulers of the land (Eli, Saul, Herod) will be brought down, while the leaders who fulfill God’s purposes (Samuel, David, Jesus) will be exalted.

**made me strong:** Literally *has exalted my horn*; cp. [2:10](1Sam.2.10). The horn of a powerful animal, such as an ox or bull, was a symbol of strength that was held high in triumph after defeating an enemy (cp. [1 Kgs 22:11](1Kgs.22.11)).
**no one besides you:** David responded similarly after receiving God’s promises concerning his kingship ([2 Sam 7:22](2Sam.7.22)).
**Rock** (cp. [2 Sam 22:2-3](2Sam.22.2-2Sam.22.3), [32](2Sam.22.32)): God provides stability and security for those who trust in him.
**proud and haughty:** Peninnah typified this attitude (see [1:6-7](1Sam.1.6-1Sam.1.7)). Hannah, by contrast, was humbly dependent on God.
Hannah celebrated God’s sovereign ability to radically reverse human circumstances.
**those who were starving are now full:** Cp. [1:7](1Sam.1.7), [18](1Sam.1.18).
The phrase **seven children** poetically means that the **childless woman** would be blessed with a house full of children (cp. [2:21](1Sam.2.21)).

**all the earth is the** **LORD’s:** God, the creator and ruler of all things, is able to change circumstances ([2:4-8](1Sam.2.4-1Sam.2.8)), protect the faithful ([2:9](1Sam.2.9)), judge the wicked, and empower his anointed king ([2:10](1Sam.2.10)).

The king was to fulfill the descriptions of [2:4-9](1Sam.2.4-1Sam.2.9) by using his God-given **power** to care for the oppressed, the hungry, and the barren (see [Ps 72:1-4](Ps.72.1-Ps.72.4), [12-14](Ps.72.12-Ps.72.14); [Prov 31:8-9](Prov.31.8-Prov.31.9)).
**he increases the strength:** See study note on 1 Sam 2:1.

**anointed one** (Hebrew *mashiakh*): This climax to Hannah’s prayer is prophetic both of Israel’s anointed kings and of God’s supreme Anointed King—the Messiah, Jesus Christ (see [12:3-5](1Sam.12.3-1Sam.12.5); [24:6](1Sam.24.6), [10](1Sam.24.10); [Ps 132:17](Ps.132.17); [Dan 9:25-26](Dan.9.25-Dan.9.26)).
**scoundrels** (Hebrew *sons of Belial*): See study note on 1:16.
**had no respect for** (literally *did not know*) **the** **LORD:** Although they were priests among God’s people, they did not acknowledge God or seek to abide by his will (cp. [Jer 2:8](Jer.2.8)).

The priests were supposed to receive their portion of the meat only after it had been boiled (see [Num 6:19](Num.6.19)). Eli’s sons disregarded God’s instructions ([1 Sam 2:13-14](1Sam.2.13-1Sam.2.14), [17](1Sam.2.17)).
God’s law stipulated that the sacrificial **animal’s fat** was the Lord’s portion and had to be **burned on the altar** first ([Lev 3:3-17](Lev.3.3-Lev.3.17)).

The clause **Samuel . . . served the** **LORD** describes the ritual service of Levites and priests (see, e.g., [Num 3:4](Num.3.4); [8:19](Num.8.19), [24](Num.8.24); [Deut 18:7](Deut.18.7)). Like Eli’s sons, Samuel was a Levite (see study note on 1 Sam 1:1). But unlike Eli’s sons, he lived up to his calling.
**He wore a linen garment like that of a priest**, as did the priests who ministered in the sanctuary (see study note on 22:18).
**Eli would bless:** Blessing was one of the functions of a priest ([Num 6:23-27](Num.6.23-Num.6.27); [Deut 10:8](Deut.10.8); [1 Chr 23:13](1Chr.23.13)). See study note on 1 Sam 1:17-18.
Eli’s weak attempts to change his sons’ behavior (cp. [2:29](1Sam.2.29)) indicate that he had raised them without discipline ([3:13](1Sam.3.13)).
**seducing . . . women:** Eli’s sons had probably been influenced by Canaanite religious practices, which included sex as part of the ritual.
**who assisted at the entrance:** See [Exod 38:8](Exod.38.8).

**God** (or *the judges*; Hebrew *’elohim*): The Hebrew verb translated **mediate** is plural here, and when *’elohim* means “God,” it often appears with a singular verb. In addition, some ancient translations render *’elohim* as “judges” here. If that is the correct translation, then the judges would **mediate for the guilty party** in a common human court. However, many Hebrew scholars believe that *’elohim* should never be translated “judges.” If this is the case, in what sense could God *mediate for the guilty party?* Possibly Eli considered the court verdict to come directly from God. God might work through his revealed law or other circumstances to either acquit or convict an individual charged with wrongdoing. Or Eli might have been referring to the sacrificial system.

The sexual immorality ([2:22](1Sam.2.22)) and gluttony ([2:12-17](1Sam.2.12-1Sam.2.17)) of Eli’s sons were **sins against the** **LORD** because they were corrupting Israel’s worship of him. No one can **intercede** for sinners who rebel so completely against God’s will (cp. [Matt 12:31](Matt.12.31)).

Eli’s sons did not **listen to their father** because the Lord had already begun to punish them by hardening their hearts (cp. [Exod 4:21](Exod.4.21); [7:3](Exod.7.3); [8:15-32](Exod.8.15-Exod.8.32); [10:27](Exod.10.27); [11:10](Exod.11.10)).
As children, both Samuel and Jesus possessed extraordinary qualities ([2:21](1Sam.2.21); see also [Luke 2:40](Luke.2.40), [52](Luke.2.52)). Samuel was one of Christ’s forerunners.
**Man of God** is another name for a prophet ([9:6](1Sam.9.6); [1 Kgs 13:1](1Kgs.13.1); [2 Kgs 1:9](2Kgs.1.9)).
By failing to stop his sons’ wickedness, Eli showed contempt for God’s **sacrifices and offerings**. Eli benefited from his sons’ activities, and God held Eli responsible for letting them continue.

**that your branch of the tribe of Levi would always be my priests:** See [Exod 29:9](Exod.29.9); [Num 25:13](Num.25.13). God would **honor** another of Aaron’s descendants (see study note on 2:35) and **despise** Eli’s family, removing them from the priesthood ([2:31-35](1Sam.2.31-1Sam.2.35)).

**live out their days:** In the Old Testament, a short life often expresses God’s disfavor, while long life represents God’s blessing (cp. [Gen 15:15](Gen.15.15); [1 Kgs 3:14](1Kgs.3.14); [Ps 91:16](Ps.91.16)).
**a faithful priest:** Zadok and his descendants later replaced Eli’s family in the priesthood ([1 Kgs 2:26-27](1Kgs.2.26-1Kgs.2.27), [35](1Kgs.2.35)).

**messages . . . were very rare . . . visions were quite uncommon:** God was not disclosing his will through prophets or priests, so the period was spiritually dark. However, that darkness was about to end when God communicated with Samuel ([3:2–4:1a](1Sam.3.2-1Sam.4.1)).
Eli was **almost blind***,* both physically and spiritually ([3:1](1Sam.3.1)).
The priests were responsible for keeping **the lamp of God** burning through the night ([Exod 27:20-21](Exod.27.20-Exod.27.21); [30:7-8](Exod.30.7-Exod.30.8)).
That Samuel **was sleeping . . . near the Ark** symbolizes his nearness to God’s presence and purpose, in contrast to Eli and his sons.

**Samuel did not yet know the** **LORD:** He lacked direct experience of the Lord. In contrast, Eli’s sons did not know the Lord (see study note on 2:12) in that they were morally and spiritually deficient.
**Eli realized:** Despite his many shortcomings, Eli was not completely without spiritual insight.
The doubling of the name calls attention to the seriousness of the moment (cp. [Gen 22:11](Gen.22.11); [Exod 3:4](Exod.3.4); [Matt 27:46](Matt.27.46); [Luke 22:31](Luke.22.31); [Acts 9:4](Acts.9.4)).
Samuel omits “LORD” (see [1 Sam 3:9](1Sam.3.9)) from his response either out of reverence for the name or because of a lingering uncertainty about who was speaking.

The phrase **a shocking thing** conveys the magnitude and severity of God’s judgment. God’s actions would also be of national significance for Israel (cp. [2 Kgs 21:12](2Kgs.21.12); [Jer 19:3](Jer.19.3)).
**his sons are blaspheming God:** They were expressing contempt for God through their actions.
**hasn’t disciplined them:** Eli rebuked his sons ([2:23-25](1Sam.2.23-1Sam.2.25)), but he did not restrain them.

Neither blood **sacrifices** nor **offerings** would be acceptable on behalf of Eli and his sons. The offerings of [Lev 4–5](Lev.4.1-Lev.5.19) were for sins committed inadvertently or unintentionally, whereas **the sins of Eli and his sons** were deliberate and rebellious.
Samuel **was afraid to tell Eli** of God’s plans for him and his family either because he respected Eli’s position or he feared for his own safety.
**proved to be reliable:** Samuel was an authentic prophet ([3:20](1Sam.3.20); see [Deut 18:21-22](Deut.18.21-Deut.18.22)).
The whole nation, **from Dan in the north to Beersheba in the south***,* acknowledged that Samuel was God’s prophet.
**confirmed as a prophet:** The reliability of Samuel’s message ([3:19](1Sam.3.19)) made it evident that God was speaking through him.
**The** **LORD continued to appear:** God reopened the lines of communication with Israel through Samuel (cp. [3:1](1Sam.3.1)).
**Shiloh:** See study note on 1:3.
The crisis surrounding the Ark of the Covenant demonstrated Israel’s need for Samuel’s leadership and fulfilled prophecies about Eli and his sons ([3:11-14](1Sam.3.11-1Sam.3.14)).
**the Philistines:** See “[The Philistines](people:ThePhilistines)” Profile.
The exact location of **Ebenezer** is unknown. It was probably just east of Aphek (see also [1 Sam 7:12](1Sam.7.12) and corresponding study note).
**Aphek** was west of Shiloh, well inland and well north of Philistine territory. By camping there, the Philistines might have been trying to seize more Israelite territory.

The Israelites were often **defeated** in war because of the sin of one individual or the entire nation ([Josh 7](Josh.7.1-Josh.7.26)). In this defeat, no one inquired whether sin was the cause; apparently no one had even asked the Lord whether they should engage the Philistines in the first place (cp. [1 Chr 14:13-16](1Chr.14.13-1Chr.14.16)). Instead, the Israelites treated the **Ark***,* the most sacred symbol of the Lord’s presence, as a charm to ward off misfortune. Carrying the Ark **into battle** was not necessarily wrong (cp. [Josh 6:2-21](Josh.6.2-Josh.6.21)), but neither would this act ensure God’s blessing and victory.
**LORD of Heaven’s Armies:** See study note on 1:3.
**enthroned between the cherubim:** A representation of God’s glorious presence hovered over the Ark in the Most Holy Place (God’s “throne room”).
The involvement of Eli’s sons, **Hophni and Phinehas***,* foreshadows the disaster that ensued (see [3:11-14](1Sam.3.11-1Sam.3.14)).
Like the Israelites, **the Philistines** regarded the **Ark** as a powerful talisman (see [4:2-3](1Sam.4.2-1Sam.4.3)) and believed that its presence in battle would mean sure **disaster** for them.
**the same gods who destroyed the Egyptians:** The Philistines, who worshiped many gods, knew of the Lord’s power. Yet they knew nothing of his nature as the one true God.
**destroyed . . . with plagues:** The Lord later showed his power against the Philistines similarly (see [5:6–6:6](1Sam.5.6)).
**30,000** was more than seven times as many as had**died** previously without the Ark ([4:2](1Sam.4.2)). The Israelites learned the hard way that the Ark was not a talisman to ward off misfortune.
That the **Ark . . . was captured** was devastating to the Israelites ([4:12-22](1Sam.4.12-1Sam.4.22)).

The deaths of **Hophni and Phinehas** fulfilled the Lord’s word to Eli ([2:34](1Sam.2.34)). Although they are the only casualties named, they were not the only Israelites who had sinned (see [7:3-6](1Sam.7.3-1Sam.7.6)).
**had torn his clothes and put dust on his head:** This description indicates **grief** and loss (e.g., [Josh 7:6](Josh.7.6); [2 Sam 1:2](2Sam.1.2); [15:32](2Sam.15.32); [Job 2:12](Job.2.12)).
**blind:** See [3:2](1Sam.3.2) and corresponding study note.

**Eli fell backward:** Either he was startled or he had a heart attack when he heard the message. Eli’s fatal fall symbolizes his family’s fall from the priesthood and the end of the abomination that his sons began ([2:12-17](1Sam.2.12-1Sam.2.17)).

**Israel’s judge:** Priesthood and judgeship were not incompatible (cp. [Exod 18:13-26](Exod.18.13-Exod.18.26); [Deut 17:8-13](Deut.17.8-Deut.17.13)). Samuel replaced Eli as Israel’s judge and provided leadership that Eli had failed to provide (see [1 Sam 7:12-17](1Sam.7.12-1Sam.7.17)).

The phrase **for forty years** incorporates Eli’s career into the conceptual and temporal framework of the book of Judges (cp. [Judg 3:11](Judg.3.11); [5:31](Judg.5.31); [8:28](Judg.8.28); [13:1](Judg.13.1)).

The name **Ichabod** contains the Hebrew word *kabod* (**glory***;* see [Exod 24:15-17](Exod.24.15-Exod.24.17)). A similar word is used to describe Eli in [1 Sam 4:18](1Sam.4.18) (Hebrew *kabed,* “heavy”). The disappearance of the Ark parallels the demise of Eli’s house. Although the Israelites experienced a stunning loss of divine glory and protection (cp. [Ezek 8–10](Ezek.8.1-Ezek.10.22); [Luke 19:41-44](Luke.19.41-Luke.19.44); [21:20-24](Luke.21.20-Luke.21.24)), God’s glorious presence would subsequently return to his people ([1 Sam 6:1-21](1Sam.6.1-1Sam.6.21); cp. [Ezek 43:1-8](Ezek.43.1-Ezek.43.8)).
**Ebenezer:** See study note on 4:1b.
**Ashdod***,* one of the five important Philistine cities (see [6:17](1Sam.6.17)), was located along the same major trade highway (the Great Trunk Road) as Aphek.

**Dagon** was one of the Philistines’ gods (see [Judg 16:23-24](Judg.16.23-Judg.16.24)). The name could be related to the Hebrew *dag* (“fish”), an appropriate name for a god of seafaring people. More likely, it reflects the Hebrew *dagan* (“grain”), suggesting a fertility or agriculture god.
**his head and hands had broken off:** A symbol of God’s supremacy over the idol ([5:7](1Sam.5.7); see also [17:51](1Sam.17.51)).

**step on its threshold:** While the Philistines might have believed that Dagon’s amputations resulted from their failure to honor the god properly, the true failure was in worshiping an idol rather than honoring the one true God ([Isa 44:6-20](Isa.44.6-Isa.44.20)).

**tumors:** The Hebrew term can mean simply “swellings.” A possible alternative translation is “hemorrhoids.” They were possibly the fatal *buboes* of bubonic plague, which attack the lower body, especially the rectal area. Rats are known carriers of the plague.
**rulers** (or *overlords*): Each of the five major Philistine cities had its own ruler ([6:16-18](1Sam.6.16-1Sam.6.18)).
**Move it:** Despite the obvious danger, the Philistines relished their captured trophy enough to relocate it rather than return it.
**Gath***,* one of the five major Philistine cities, was nearby.
God often used **great panic** to incapacitate and overwhelm Israel’s enemies ([14:15](1Sam.14.15), [20](1Sam.14.20); [Deut 7:23](Deut.7.23); [Ezek 22:5](Ezek.22.5); [Amos 3:9](Amos.3.9)).
**Ekron***,* another of the five major Philistine cities (see [6:17](1Sam.6.17)), was just five miles north of Gath.
**priests and diviners:** Divination was a part of Philistine religion (cp. [28:7](1Sam.28.7); [Deut 18:10-14](Deut.18.10-Deut.18.14)).

It is unlikely the Philistines were aware of Israelite worship regulations. A Philistine **guilt offering** would have been a payment to the deity in an attempt to avert his wrath (contrast the notion of atonement from [Lev 16](Lev.16.1-Lev.16.34)).
**rats:** See study note on 5:6.
The Philistines had thought they could overcome the Lord by fighting harder ([4:9](1Sam.4.9)). They had defeated the Israelites, but they now realized that they could not defeat Israel’s God.
**shut their calves away:** If the **cows** went against their maternal nature and left their calves to take the Ark to Israel, it would prove that the plague was from Israel’s God ([6:9](1Sam.6.9)).
**Beth-shemesh** was the closest Israelite town to Ekron ([5:10](1Sam.5.10)).
**Harvesting wheat** was usually done in May or June.

This **burnt offering** could have been for forgiveness of sin (see [7:9-10](1Sam.7.9-1Sam.7.10); [Lev 1:3-17](Lev.1.3-Lev.1.17)), but it was more likely a freewill expression of love or thanksgiving (see [Lev 22:18-22](Lev.22.18-Lev.22.22)).

Providentially, **the Ark** had arrived in **Beth-shemesh** ([6:13](1Sam.6.13)), which was a Levite city ([Josh 21:13-16](Josh.21.13-Josh.21.16)). The **men of the tribe of Levi** who lived there could safely move the Ark (see [Num 4:15](Num.4.15)).
**guilt offering:** See study note on 6:3.

**Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron:** These five major Philistine cities were located on or near the Great Trunk Road. This major ancient trade route connected Egypt with Mesopotamia via the coastal plain of Canaan. Each city was governed by a king-like ruler ([6:16](1Sam.6.16)).
**seventy men: Beth-shemesh** was a small village.

**because they looked into the Ark:** Physical contact with the Ark was prohibited ([Num 4:15](Num.4.15); [2 Sam 6:6-8](2Sam.6.6-2Sam.6.8)), as was looking inside it ([Num 4:20](Num.4.20)). Those who were killed lacked reverence for God’s holiness.
**Who is able to stand?** Even God’s people were not immune to his wrath when his holiness was violated.
**Where can we send the Ark?** When faced with God’s holiness, the Israelites echoed the distress of the pagan Philistines ([6:2](1Sam.6.2)).
**Kiriath-jearim** was nearby, about ten miles northeast of Beth-shemesh.
The **men of Kiriath-jearim** who transported **the Ark** and **Eleazar** were probably Levites (see [6:15](1Sam.6.15); [Num 1:47-51](Num.1.47-Num.1.51)).
**in charge of it:** The same verb describes the Levites’ duty of guarding the Tabernacle ([Num 1:53](Num.1.53); [3:7](Num.3.7)).
**Twenty years** covers the time until Samuel assembled the people at Mizpah ([7:5-6](1Sam.7.5-1Sam.7.6)). David later brought the Ark to Jerusalem ([2 Sam 6:1-19](2Sam.6.1-2Sam.6.19)).
The change in the people’s standing with God, not the presence of the Ark (see [4:3-11](1Sam.4.3-1Sam.4.11)), led Israel to victory against the Philistines.
People cannot expect God’s blessing unless they **get rid of** what is contrary to his will (see [Gen 35:2](Gen.35.2); [Josh 24:14](Josh.24.14)).

**Ashtoreth** was the Canaanite goddess of fertility associated with Baal ([1 Sam 7:4](1Sam.7.4)). Worship of Canaanite deities was an ongoing problem throughout Israel’s history. The people started worshiping idols during the twenty-year period mentioned in [7:2](1Sam.7.2), or perhaps they had done so ever since the days of the judges ([8:8](1Sam.8.8); [Judg 6:25](Judg.6.25); cp. [Amos 5:25-26](Amos.5.25-Amos.5.26)). Israel’s devastating defeat by the Philistines was due not only to the sins of Eli’s two sons but to several generations of unfaithfulness to God.
**Mizpah** was an administrative center and rallying point for the nation (see [7:16](1Sam.7.16); [10:17](1Sam.10.17); [Judg 20:1](Judg.20.1)).
**I will pray . . . for you:** Eli’s question in [1 Sam 2:25](1Sam.2.25) is answered here; Samuel was the intercessor Israel needed.
**drew water . . . poured it out:** This type of ceremony is not mentioned elsewhere in the Old Testament.

At times Israelites **went without food** to express grief or to seek the Lord’s favor ([2 Sam 1:12](2Sam.1.12); [12:22-23](2Sam.12.22-2Sam.12.23); [1 Kgs 21:27](1Kgs.21.27); [Ezra 8:21-23](Ezra.8.21-Ezra.8.23); [Neh 9:1](Neh.9.1); [Esth 4:3](Esth.4.3), [16](Esth.4.16); [Joel 2:12](Joel.2.12); cp. [Luke 2:37](Luke.2.37); [Acts 13:2-3](Acts.13.2-Acts.13.3); [14:23](Acts.14.23)).

To have **Samuel** as **Israel’s judge** was refreshing compared to Eli’s failed leadership (see [1 Sam 4:18](1Sam.4.18) and corresponding study note) and the leadership of some other judges (e.g., Gideon, [Judg 8:22-27](Judg.8.22-Judg.8.27); Jephthah, [Judg 11:30–12:7](Judg.11.30-Judg.12.7); and Samson, [Judg 13:1–16:21](Judg.13.1-Judg.16.21)).
The **whole burnt offering** was probably for forgiveness of sin (see [Lev 1:1-4](Lev.1.1-Lev.1.4)).
**The** **LORD answered** with a forceful thunderclap ([1 Sam 7:10](1Sam.7.10)).

**voice of thunder:** See [2:10](1Sam.2.10). God often used similar tactics to throw Israel’s enemies into **confusion** and defeat them (e.g., [Exod 14:24](Exod.14.24); [23:27](Exod.23.27); [Josh 10:10](Josh.10.10); [Judg 4:15](Judg.4.15)).

**Ebenezer:** The location of this **stone** memorial is unknown. The Philistines had defeated Israel and captured the Ark at a place with the same name ([4:1](1Sam.4.1); [5:1](1Sam.5.1)). Samuel erected this memorial to commemorate God’s help in turning the tide against the Philistine attacks.
The Philistines were quiet **for some time**—until Saul became king (see [13:5](1Sam.13.5)).
God’s **powerful hand***,* not Samuel’s giftedness, was the key factor in Israel’s deliverance from the Philistines.

The **Amorites** had inhabited Canaan and the region east of the Jordan before Israel’s conquest of the Promised Land (see [Gen 15:16](Gen.15.16); [Deut 3:8](Deut.3.8); [Josh 2:10](Josh.2.10)). Some Amorites remained in the area after the conquest (see [2 Sam 21:2](2Sam.21.2)).
**judge for the rest of his life:** Once Saul became king (ch [10](1Sam.10.1-1Sam.10.27)), Samuel’s role was more judicial than military.

**Bethel** and **Mizpah** were places of national assembly in the judges era ([Judg 20:1](Judg.20.1), [18](Judg.20.18), [26](Judg.20.26); [21:1-2](Judg.21.1-Judg.21.2)). Bethel’s significance went back to the days of Abraham ([Gen 12:8](Gen.12.8); [13:3-4](Gen.13.3-Gen.13.4); [28:10-22](Gen.28.10-Gen.28.22); [35:1-15](Gen.35.1-Gen.35.15)).

**Gilgal***,* located near Jericho, had been a sacred place since Joshua’s day ([Josh 4:19-24](Josh.4.19-Josh.4.24); [5:2-10](Josh.5.2-Josh.5.10)). From this circuit, Samuel influenced “all the people of Israel” ([1 Sam 10:17](1Sam.10.17)).
**Ramah** was Samuel’s hometown (see [1:1](1Sam.1.1)).

During Israel’s transition to a monarchy, neither God ([8:7-9](1Sam.8.7-1Sam.8.9)) nor Samuel ([12:1-25](1Sam.12.1-1Sam.12.25)) was pleased by the people’s demand for a king. Saul, the first king (chs [9–11](1Sam.9.1-1Sam.11.15)), failed in his role (chs [13–31](1Sam.13.1-1Sam.31.13)) and fulfilled Samuel’s warnings (see [8:10-18](1Sam.8.10-1Sam.8.18); cp. [16:1-13](1Sam.16.1-1Sam.16.13)).
Samuel’s two **oldest sons** functioned as judges **in Beersheba***,* fifty miles south of their father’s home.
**they were not like their father:** They were more like Eli’s two sons ([2:12-17](1Sam.2.12-1Sam.2.17)). Their corruption was a primary reason the era of the judges ended.

**you are now old, and your sons are not like you:** Judges tended to be local leaders; kings, as national leaders, were more capable of uniting a whole nation in times of crisis ([8:20](1Sam.8.20)). However, a spiritual problem underlay the request for a king ([8:7-8](1Sam.8.7-1Sam.8.8)).
**Other nations,** such as Egypt and Sumer, had monarchies for almost 2,000 years before Samuel’s time.
**Samuel was displeased:** He probably felt personally rejected ([8:7](1Sam.8.7)).

**Do everything they say:** God rarely instructed a prophet to heed the voice of the errant populace. The will of the people and the will of God would converge in King David (see [2 Sam 7:8-17](2Sam.7.8-2Sam.7.17)).
**they are rejecting me:** Their rejection of judgeship was a deeper rejection of God’s rule and sovereignty (see also [1 Sam 12:1-17](1Sam.12.1-1Sam.12.17)).

**followed other gods:** The people’s request for a king was tantamount to idolatry. Israel’s monarchy was a divine concession rather than a divine gift. Kingship or any other human institution becomes idolatrous when it replaces trust in God.
These verses list the disadvantages of kingship. Each sentence begins with something the king would take. A king would be a confiscator, not just a protector.
While the people wanted a king to *judge* them, Samuel warned that the king would **reign over** them. They wanted a leader but received a ruler.
The king would take people as well as possessions.

A **tenth** of the harvest was already required as a sacred donation to support God’s Temple and servants ([Deut 12:6](Deut.12.6), [17-18](Deut.12.17-Deut.12.18); [14:22-29](Deut.14.22-Deut.14.29); [26:12-15](Deut.26.12-Deut.26.15)). The king would demand an additional tenth, a burdensome amount given the uncertainties of agriculture.
**you will be his slaves:** By demanding a king, the people whose ancestors had once been slaves in Egypt were risking a new enslavement (cp. [1 Kgs 12:1-20](1Kgs.12.1-1Kgs.12.20)).
The people would **beg for relief** as their ancestors had done in Egypt under another punishing and exacting ruler (see [Exod 3:7](Exod.3.7)).

God had set Israel apart from the nations ([Lev 20:26](Lev.20.26); [Num 23:9](Num.23.9)). By insisting on a king and desiring to **be like the nations***,* they were rejecting God’s plan (see [1 Sam 8:5-7](1Sam.8.5-1Sam.8.7); cp. [Deut 17:14](Deut.17.14)).
**judge us and lead us into battle:** Kings performed three basic functions: (1) waging offensive and defensive war, (2) administering law, and (3) ensuring economic well-being.
**repeated to the** **LORD:** The role of a prophet included bringing the people’s case before God (cp. [Num 27:5](Num.27.5)).
**give them a king:** See study note on 8:7; cp. [Rom 1:24-26](Rom.1.24-Rom.1.26).

Saul’s rise to power involved a threefold sequence: (1) his secret anointing by Samuel ([9:1–10:16](1Sam.9.1-1Sam.10.16)), (2) his selection by lot ([10:17-27](1Sam.10.17-1Sam.10.27)), and (3) his victory over the Ammonites ([11:1-15](1Sam.11.1-1Sam.11.15)). See also study note on 13:1–16:13.
**influential man named Kish:** Saul came from a wealthy family.
Saul’s mere appearance—**most handsome . . . taller than anyone else**—inspired loyalty among the people (see [10:23](1Sam.10.23); cp. [16:12](1Sam.16.12); [2 Sam 14:25-26](2Sam.14.25-2Sam.14.26)).
**Zuph***,* which was probably located in Ephraim, was Samuel’s home region ([1:1](1Sam.1.1)). God’s providence led Saul there.
The phrase **man of God** was used to describe a prophet ([2:27](1Sam.2.27); also [Deut 33:1](Deut.33.1); [Josh 14:6](Josh.14.6); [1 Kgs 13:1-32](1Kgs.13.1-1Kgs.13.32)).

**anything to offer him:** Evidently, it was customary to take a gift when one sought the help of a prophet (cp. [1 Kgs 14:2-3](1Kgs.14.2-1Kgs.14.3); [2 Kgs 5:5](2Kgs.5.5), [15](2Kgs.5.15); [8:8](2Kgs.8.8)). Some false prophets demanded gifts in return for their services ([Mic 3:11](Mic.3.11)). Saul’s concern might reflect the spiritual ignorance of thinking that advice from a prophet of God could be purchased ([Acts 8:20](Acts.8.20)).
Leaders of a community would normally convene for business at the **town gates** (cp. [Ruth 4:1-2](Ruth.4.1-Ruth.4.2)).
**take part in a public sacrifice:** Samuel is one of very few individuals in whom prophetic and priestly ministries unite (also Moses, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Jesus).

**place of worship** (literally *high place*): An open-air altar or platform on a hill near the city gate. High places easily became sites for pagan idolatry (see [Num 33:52](Num.33.52); [1 Kgs 15:14](1Kgs.15.14); [22:43](1Kgs.22.43); [2 Kgs 12:3](2Kgs.12.3); [14:4](2Kgs.14.4); [15:4](2Kgs.15.4), [35](2Kgs.15.35)).
**to eat:** Part of a sacrifice made during worship was burned on the altar, while the remainder was eaten in a ceremonial feast by the **guests** (see also [1:4](1Sam.1.4)).
**to bless the food:** As a Levite, Samuel’s priestly role included offering blessings (see [Deut 10:8](Deut.10.8); [21:5](Deut.21.5)).

God’s directive to **anoint him** (by pouring olive oil on the head) marked Saul’s elevation in status and consecration for a special purpose (see [Exod 30:22-33](Exod.30.22-Exod.30.33); [Lev 8:12](Lev.8.12); [1 Kgs 19:16](1Kgs.19.16); [Isa 45:1](Isa.45.1)).

**He will rescue them:** As they had requested ([1 Sam 8:20](1Sam.8.20); cp. [Judg 13:5](Judg.13.5)). David eventually subdued **the Philistines** ([2 Sam 5:17-25](2Sam.5.17-2Sam.5.25); [8:1](2Sam.8.1); [21:15](2Sam.21.15), [18-22](2Sam.21.18-2Sam.21.22)).
**for I have . . . heard their cry** (cp. [Exod 3:7-9](Exod.3.7-Exod.3.9)): The Philistines were again threatening to conquer Israel and demand homage from them as vassals.

**the smallest tribe:** Saul tried to downplay Benjamin’s prominence, but they were powerful warriors ([Judg 20:14-31](Judg.20.14-Judg.20.31); cp. study note on 1 Sam 10:17). What better tribe to lead in battle?
**least important of all the families:** Cp. [9:1](1Sam.9.1).
A typical house had a flat **roof** that was used for a variety of purposes, such as sleeping in warm weather (see [Deut 22:8](Deut.22.8); [2 Kgs 4:10](2Kgs.4.10)).
Samuel later repeated this process by anointing David with **olive oil** ([16:13](1Sam.16.13)).
The people of Israel did not belong to the king but to the Lord. The king was to act as manager rather than owner (cp. [8:10-18](1Sam.8.10-1Sam.8.18)).
These three “signs” were to convince a reluctant Saul ([9:21](1Sam.9.21)) that he had in fact been chosen to be king.
**Rachel’s tomb at Zelzah:** See [Gen 35:16-20](Gen.35.16-Gen.35.20); the precise location is unknown.
**oak of Tabor:** This location, somewhere in Benjamin, is not to be confused with the village of the same name in Zebulun ([1 Chr 6:77](1Chr.6.77)).
**Bethel:** See study note on 1 Sam 7:16.

**Gibeah of God,** Saul’s hometown ([10:26](1Sam.10.26)), had been a lawless city ([Judg 19–21](Judg.19.1-Judg.21.25)). Nowhere else is it described as being “of God.” This description might point to God’s ownership of the town despite the occupation of the **Philistines**.
**band:** Prophets often lived in groups (e.g., [2 Kgs 2:3](2Kgs.2.3)).
**harp . . . lyre:** Ancient prophets sometimes used musical instruments to stimulate and accompany **prophesying** (e.g., [2 Kgs 3:15](2Kgs.3.15)).
**different person:** Saul would become a spiritual and charismatic national leader (cp. [1 Sam 16:14](1Sam.16.14)).
**for God is with you:** God’s presence empowered Saul to carry out his responsibilities.
**Gilgal:** See study note on 7:16.
**wait for seven days:** Saul apparently fulfilled this instruction in [11:14-15](1Sam.11.14-1Sam.11.15) (cp. [13:8](1Sam.13.8)).
**a new heart:** God gave Saul courage and strength, helping him overcome his hesitancy and enabling him to be king ([10:6](1Sam.10.6)).

**the Spirit of God came powerfully upon Saul:** See “[The Spirit’s Presence](themes:TheSpiritsPresence)” Theme Note; see also [11:6](1Sam.11.6); [Judg 14:6](Judg.14.6), [19](Judg.14.19); [15:14](Judg.15.14); cp. [Acts 2:17-18](Acts.2.17-Acts.2.18), [39](Acts.2.39)).
When **Saul . . . began to prophesy***,* it was a clear sign that he had been chosen to lead Israel (see also [1 Sam 19:18-23](1Sam.19.18-1Sam.19.23)).

**Those who knew Saul** might have known him to be nonreligious and thus an unlikely candidate for prophet. Their surprise might indicate disappointment at receiving a prophet instead of a king (cp. [John 6:14-15](John.6.14-John.6.15)).

**“Can anyone become a prophet, no matter who his father is?”** Unlike priests and kings, prophets never inherited their office. Possibly the people were asking why Saul, whose well-to-do father was well known, would associate himself with a group of people who had no pedigree.
Perhaps **Saul didn’t tell his uncle** because he had lingering uncertainty about what had transpired.
An earlier generation had gathered at **Mizpah** to decimate the tribe of Benjamin ([Judg 20:1-4](Judg.20.1-Judg.20.4)), making the city an ironic place to inaugurate a man of Benjamin as king.
**rescued you . . . from all of the nations:** Israel did not need a human king to rescue them; they needed God, but they had rejected him ([10:19](1Sam.10.19)).
**rejected your God:** See also [8:7](1Sam.8.7). Israel was rejecting God’s ability to protect and save them.
**Clans** are subdivisions of **tribes**.
**rights and duties of a king:** See [Deut 17:14-20](Deut.17.14-Deut.17.20).
**He wrote them:** Cp. [Exod 24:4](Exod.24.4); [Josh 24:26](Josh.24.26).
Samuel placed the document **before the** **LORD**—presumably in the Tabernacle. This position showed that God would honor those who lived by the covenant and punish those who violated it.
Saul proved his capacity for leadership by tolerating opposition and rescuing the town of Jabesh-gilead.
**whose hearts God had touched:** God gave people confidence in Saul’s ability to lead (cp. [10:9](1Sam.10.9)).
These men were **scoundrels** (cp. [2:12](1Sam.2.12)) because they **scorned** God’s chosen king.

**Gifts** were given to show homage ([Gen 32:13](Gen.32.13), [18](Gen.32.18), [20](Gen.32.20)), political friendship ([2 Kgs 20:12](2Kgs.20.12)), or submission ([Judg 3:15](Judg.3.15), [17](Judg.3.17)).

**ignored them:** Saul’s self-restraint while being insulted was a sign of maturity. In contrast, [Proverbs 16:14](Prov.16.14) speaks of a king’s potentially explosive rage when somebody crosses him. See also [1 Sam 11:12-13](1Sam.11.12-1Sam.11.13).

**\[Nahash . . . Jabesh-gilead\]:** See NLT note. Whether this paragraph was part of the original text is uncertain, but it provides historical context for [11:1-15](1Sam.11.1-1Sam.11.15) (e.g., [11:2](1Sam.11.2)).
Saul’s kingship was confirmed through a military victory, the very reason the people wanted a king ([8:20](1Sam.8.20)).

**Ammon** (see [Gen 19:38](Gen.19.38)), located on the east side of the Jordan, represented a threat to Israel similar to the Philistines to the southwest (see also [Judg 10:6–11:33](Judg.10.6-Judg.11.33)).
**Make a treaty with us:** Cp. [Josh 9](Josh.9.1-Josh.9.27); [2 Sam 10:19](2Sam.10.19).

**gouge out the right eye:** Mutilation of captured soldiers was a common practice in the ancient Near East. These disfigured soldiers would have lost all depth perception, seriously curtailing their potential for fighting in a revolt.
Nahash agreed to grant a reprieve of **seven days,** reflecting his arrogant confidence of victory and his desire to humiliate Israel as much as possible.
Not to participate would indicate rejection of the leadership of both **Saul** as king and **Samuel** as prophet.
**Bezek** was about fourteen miles west of Jabesh-gilead.
The narrator’s use of the terms **Israel** and **Judah** anticipates the later division of the kingdom ([1 Kgs 12](1Kgs.12.1-1Kgs.12.33)).
**No one will be executed:** This was a time for rejoicing, not revenge.

**renew the kingdom:** “Renew” indicates that someone or something had deteriorated or had been damaged (cp. [Ps 51:10](Ps.51.10)). Whatever effect the scoundrels ([1 Sam 10:27](1Sam.10.27); [11:12](1Sam.11.12)) might have had in undermining the people’s confidence was now rectified by Saul’s victory over the Ammonites.
The **solemn ceremony before the** **LORD** acknowledged Saul’s sovereignty as king while affirming that the Lord was Israel’s true King.

**Peace offerings** were common on historic occasions that inaugurated important institutions (see [Exod 24:5](Exod.24.5); [Lev 9:4](Lev.9.4), [18](Lev.9.18), [22](Lev.9.22); [1 Kgs 8:63-64](1Kgs.8.63-1Kgs.8.64)).

The reaffirmation of Saul’s kingship at Gilgal ([11:12-15](1Sam.11.12-1Sam.11.15)) was the final step in his installation as king. The event was a fitting occasion for Samuel’s farewell address as leader of Israel.
God’s **anointed one** was Saul (see [9:16](1Sam.9.16)).
**Whose ox or donkey:** Cp. [Num 16:15](Num.16.15).
**have I stolen?** In contrast to the behavior of kings ([1 Sam 8:11-16](1Sam.8.11-1Sam.8.16)).
**Have I ever taken a bribe and perverted justice?** No, but Samuel’s sons did ([8:3](1Sam.8.3)).

**my hands are clean:** Samuel’s life and leadership before Israel had been above reproach (cp. [1 Cor 9:1-14](1Cor.9.1-1Cor.9.14); [2 Cor 7:2](2Cor.7.2); [11:7-9](2Cor.11.7-2Cor.11.9); [1 Thes 2:1-12](1Thess.2.1-1Thess.2.12)). Saul, David, and Solomon—kings rather than prophetic judges—would not be able to make this claim.
In [12:1-5](1Sam.12.1-1Sam.12.5), Samuel put himself on trial and was found innocent. In [12:6-25](1Sam.12.6-1Sam.12.25), he put the nation on trial and found it guilty.
**Moses and Aaron** were not self-made leaders but were **appointed** by God as leaders.
**handed them over:** See [Judg 3:8](Judg.3.8); [4:1-3](Judg.4.1-Judg.4.3).

**the king of Moab:** See [Judg 3:12](Judg.3.12). Not all of Israel’s enemies in the era of the judges are listed (e.g., the Ammonites and Midianites). This list is representative to emphasize the highs and lows of that era.

**Then they cried to the** **LORD:** Sometimes only suffering turns people’s hearts toward God. During the period of the judges, Israel repeatedly went through cycles of sin, oppression, repentance, and rescue.
**Baal and Ashtoreth:** When people turn **away from** God, they inevitably turn to idols (see [7:3](1Sam.7.3); [Judg 2:13](Judg.2.13); [10:6](Judg.10.6)).

An attitude such as **if you will rescue us** turns **worship** into a debased bargain, in which God must perform some action to a person’s liking. God deserves obedience and *worship* because he is God, not because of favors he can perform.
As in [12:9](1Sam.12.9), this list of leaders is representative.
**Bedan:** Greek and Syriac versions read *Barak* (see [Judg 4:6-24](Judg.4.6-Judg.4.24); [5:1](Judg.5.1), [12](Judg.5.12), [15](Judg.5.15)). The identity of this judge remains uncertain.
**you were afraid of Nahash:** Israel’s trouble with Nahash apparently preceded [11:1-11](1Sam.11.1-1Sam.11.11) (cp. [8:5](1Sam.8.5), [20](1Sam.8.20); [10:27](1Sam.10.27)).
Even though the Israelites’ **request** amounted to a rejection of God as king, **the** **LORD . . . granted** it (see study notes on 8:7 and 8:8).

To show that even under a monarchy Israel must still keep its covenant with the Lord—who was always to be their true king—Samuel echoed language from the Sinai covenant (e.g., [Exod 19:5-6](Exod.19.5-Exod.19.6); [Lev 26](Lev.26.1-Lev.26.46); [Deut 30:11-20](Deut.30.11-Deut.30.20)).
**Worship** is meaningless if it does not result in obedience.

The **wheat harvest** occurred in late spring or early summer, when little or no rain fell in Israel. **Thunder and rain** would thus demonstrate God’s power as a sign of the people’s wickedness in asking for a king.
**terrified:** Cp. [Exod 19:16](Exod.19.16).

The people asked Samuel to intercede for them (see also [7:8](1Sam.7.8)) rather than praying themselves probably because they were out of fellowship with God (note the use of **your God** rather than “our God”).
**added to our sins:** The sins included idol worship ([12:21](1Sam.12.21); see study note on 8:8).
**worthless . . . totally useless:** Israel was slow to learn this lesson (e.g., [Isa 40:18-26](Isa.40.18-Isa.40.26); [44:9-20](Isa.44.9-Isa.44.20)).

**because that would dishonor his great name:** God will never contradict his own character and detract from his glory (see also [Isa 37:35](Isa.37.35); [43:25](Isa.43.25); [48:9-11](Isa.48.9-Isa.48.11)). Therefore, he always keeps his covenant promises, even if his people do not.

**his very own people:** Israel is God’s treasured possession (see [Exod 19:5](Exod.19.5); [Deut 9:25-29](Deut.9.25-Deut.9.29)). He will never abandon them (see [Rom 11:1-5](Rom.11.1-Rom.11.5), [25-32](Rom.11.25-Rom.11.32)).
**I will continue to teach you:** Samuel was both intercessor and educator.
Although this address marked the end of Samuel’s political leadership, he continued his spiritual ministry for some time (e.g., [19:24](1Sam.19.24)).

**swept away:** David later used this same Hebrew verb for Saul’s death ([26:10](1Sam.26.10), “die . . . in battle”) and for his own possible death at Saul’s hands ([27:1](1Sam.27.1), “get me”). The warning would remain in force throughout Israel’s history as a monarchy.

Saul’s fall from power involved a threefold sequence, as had his rise to power (see study note on 9:1–11:15): (1) He offered the sacrifices himself and did not wait for Samuel ([13:1-14](1Sam.13.1-1Sam.13.14)); (2) he made a rash oath that put Jonathan’s life in danger ([14:1-46](1Sam.14.1-1Sam.14.46)); and (3) he failed to obey God by eliminating the Amalekites and their belongings ([15:1-35](1Sam.15.1-1Sam.15.35)).
For the kings of Israel and Judah, Scripture normally records the age of ascension and the length of reign (e.g., [2 Sam 5:4-5](2Sam.5.4-2Sam.5.5); [1 Kgs 14:21](1Kgs.14.21)).
**thirty years old:** The number represents a plausible age for Saul’s ascension. The Hebrew text and most Greek manuscripts omit the number , making it difficult to know the original wording.

**reigned for forty-two years:** See NLT textual note. Most scholars agree that something has fallen out of the original manuscript, most likely due to a copyist’s error. The majority of English translations have *forty-two* based on the approximate number in [Acts 13:21](Acts.13.21).

Earlier, **Saul** had employed 330,000 troops to fight against a much less formidable foe ([11:8](1Sam.11.8)). The selection here of **3,000 special troops** probably does not reflect overconfidence (cp. [Josh 7:3-4](Josh.7.3-Josh.7.4)). Rather, Saul likely recognized the need for a smaller, highly trained, elite militia to deal with the troublesome Philistines (see [1 Sam 14:52](1Sam.14.52)).
**Micmash** was located in Benjamin about two miles northwest of Saul’s home in Gibeah.
**Geba** was located between Jonathan’s forces at Gibeah and Saul’s forces at Micmash. A deep gorge separated Geba and Micmash (see [13:23](1Sam.13.23); [14:5](1Sam.14.5)).

**The ram’s horn** (Hebrew *shofar*) was used to raise a signal—e.g., to muster an army ([Judg 3:27](Judg.3.27)). For other uses, see [Lev 25:9](Lev.25.9); [2 Sam 6:15](2Sam.6.15); [15:10](2Sam.15.10); [18:16](2Sam.18.16); [20:1](2Sam.20.1); [Hos 5:8](Hos.5.8); [Joel 2:15](Joel.2.15).

Non-Israelites often used the term **Hebrews** disdainfully (see [1 Sam 14:11](1Sam.14.11); [29:3](1Sam.29.3); see also [Gen 39:14](Gen.39.14); [43:32](Gen.43.32)). Saul might have used it to strike a nerve and arouse the people’s pride in their identity.
**Saul had destroyed:** The commander in chief often got credit for what his soldiers accomplished.
Saul’s kingship had been reaffirmed at **Gilgal** ([11:15](1Sam.11.15)). Now the Lord would reject his kingship there because of his disobedience ([13:7-14](1Sam.13.7-1Sam.13.14)).
The Israelites were massively outnumbered, hence their fearful responses.
The Philistine army’s **3,000 chariots** and **6,000 charioteers** indicate Israel’s underdog status. Nowhere in 1 Samuel is Israel said to have had any chariots (see study note on 13:19-22).
The **land of Gad and Gilead** ran the length of Transjordan (the region just east of the Jordan River).
**seven days . . . as Samuel had instructed:** This instruction most likely was not the instruction in [10:8](1Sam.10.8) but an unrecorded instruction on a separate occasion (see study note on 10:8).

**the burnt offering and the peace offerings:** These general-purpose offerings (see [Exod 24:5](Exod.24.5); [32:6](Exod.32.6); [Num 10:10](Num.10.10); [15:8](Num.15.8); [Deut 27:6-7](Deut.27.6-Deut.27.7)) were always offered on a solemn occasion filled with either danger or joy. Typically, only priests were to offer these sacrifices (but see study note on 1 Sam 13:13).
**meet and welcome:** Saul seemed unaware he had done anything wrong.
**What is this you have done?** Samuel’s question was a rebuke, not a request for information (cp. [Gen 3:13](Gen.3.13)).

**asked for the** **LORD’s help:** The purpose of the **burnt offering** was to entreat God to grant victory in battle. Samuel himself had offered a similar sacrifice, which did lead to victory in battle (see [7:7-11](1Sam.7.7-1Sam.7.11)). But Samuel, unlike Saul, served in a priestly role.

**the command the** **LORD . . . gave you:** Other kings offered sacrifices without censure (David, [2 Sam 6:13](2Sam.6.13), [17-18](2Sam.6.17-2Sam.6.18); Solomon, [1 Kgs 3:15](1Kgs.3.15); [8:64](1Kgs.8.64); Ahaz, [2 Kgs 16:12-13](2Kgs.16.12-2Kgs.16.13)), as did judges (Gideon, [Judg 6:26](Judg.6.26)), illustrating that on occasion non-priests could conduct sacrifices in a way that pleased the Lord. However, Samuel, God’s prophet, had given Saul the order to wait (see study note on 1 Sam 13:8).

**a man after his own heart:** This prophecy pertains to David (see also [Acts 13:22](Acts.13.22)) rather than to Saul’s son Jonathan. The rejection of Saul was also the rejection of his family dynasty.
**only 600 were left:** Most of the 3,000 troops ([13:2](1Sam.13.2)) had abandoned Saul ([13:6-7](1Sam.13.6-1Sam.13.7)).

Armies would send out **raiding parties** to plunder and sow panic among the enemy. These raiders embarked north (**Ophrah**), west (**Beth-horon**), and east (**Zeboim**), but not south, where Israelite strength was consolidated and where the terrain did not allow easy movement of forces (see study note on 13:23).

**no blacksmiths:** The Philistines kept the Israelites unarmed by gaining a monopoly on the iron necessary to make weapons. Iron technology had not existed long in Canaan; it might have developed in the Aegean area, and metalworking skills were possibly introduced into Canaan through seafaring peoples, including the Philistines.
**The pass at Micmash** was a strategic passage through the canyon that separated Micmash from Geba, Gibeah, and other towns to the south.

Saul’s behavior in this chapter further justifies his dismissal as king ([13:8-14](1Sam.13.8-1Sam.13.14); see also ch [15](1Sam.15.1-1Sam.15.35)). Saul was alienated from both Samuel and his heroic son Jonathan. [Chapter 14](1Sam.14.1-1Sam.14.52) anticipates the significant role that Jonathan played in the transition from Saul’s kingship to David’s.
Jonathan again fought in his father’s battles (see also [13:2-4](1Sam.13.2-1Sam.13.4); ch [31](1Sam.31.1-1Sam.31.13)).
**armor bearer:** See study note on 16:21.
**Jonathan did not tell his father** because he knew that Saul would not grant permission for the dangerous plan. But he also knew that Saul wanted no one—not even his own son—to upstage him.
**camped:** Saul’s inactivity contrasts with Jonathan’s initiative (see also [22:6](1Sam.22.6)).

**Ahijah the priest** was an adviser who could give Saul divine guidance through **the ephod** ([14:18-19](1Sam.14.18-1Sam.14.19); see also [2:18](1Sam.2.18) and corresponding study note; [23:9-10](1Sam.23.9-1Sam.23.10)).
**son of Eli:** Saul, the rejected king ([13:13-14](1Sam.13.13-1Sam.13.14)), kept in his company a priest from the rejected priesthood ([2:27-36](1Sam.2.27-1Sam.2.36)).
The Philistines had already secured this area ([13:23](1Sam.13.23)), so Jonathan and his armor bearer had to move carefully.
**pagans** (literally *uncircumcised*): A disdainful term for enemies of Israel (see also [17:36](1Sam.17.36); [31:4](1Sam.31.4)).

**Perhaps:** Jonathan had no guarantee of survival, but he was certain that God could grant them victory despite the odds. Victory was in God’s hands; Jonathan offered himself as an instrument God could use.
**many warriors or only a few:** Jonathan knew what Gideon had learned many years earlier (see [Judg 7:2-8](Judg.7.2-Judg.7.8)).
**Hebrews:** See study note on 13:3.
**crawling out of their holes:** See [13:6](1Sam.13.6).

**panic broke out:** This parallel with the Gideon story depicts Jonathan as a judge-like figure (cp. [Judg 7:19-22](Judg.7.19-Judg.7.22)). God had not anointed or expressly gifted Jonathan to be leader, yet God used him to rescue his people.
**raiding parties:** See study note on 1 Sam 13:17-18.

**Bring . . . Israelites:** See NLT textual note; the Greek text is likely original. The Ark remained at Kiriath-jearim for twenty years ([7:2](1Sam.7.2)), and it was never used for getting information about the future, as the ephod was (see study note on 2:18).

**Previously***,* a large group of Israelites had gone into **hiding** out of fear ([13:6-7](1Sam.13.6-1Sam.13.7)). Others might have joined **the Philistine army**. However, the statement that they **revolted** when the opportunity arose suggests they might have been taken as prisoners of war and forced into the Philistines’ service.
It was God, not Saul, who **saved Israel***;* Jonathan was just a willing instrument in the Lord’s hands.
**Beth-aven** was due west of Micmash (see [13:5](1Sam.13.5)). The Israelites forced the Philistines to retreat all the way to Aijalon that day (see [14:31](1Sam.14.31)).

With his **oath***,* Saul forced abstinence from food on men who were already hungry and exhausted from battle. This oath was probably a pagan-like attempt to manipulate God into giving them a favorable result (cp. notes on Exod 23:26; 25:22; 32:4).
That Saul said **my enemies** rather than “our enemies” reflects his self-centered pride.

**made trouble:** Joshua had used this verb in speaking with Achan ([Josh 7:25](Josh.7.25)), and Jephthah had used it with his innocent daughter ([Judg 11:35](Judg.11.35)). Saul’s foolish oath limited Israel’s victory ([1 Sam 14:30](1Sam.14.30)) and put his son’s life at risk (see also [Josh 6:18](Josh.6.18); [1 Chr 2:7](1Chr.2.7)).
**Aijalon:** If the Philistines fled along the likely route through Beth-horon, then the Israelites kept up the pursuit for close to twenty miles.

The men were famished, so they ate meat **without draining the blood.** This act violated God’s law (see [Lev 17:10-14](Lev.17.10-Lev.17.14)) and thus constituted **sinning against the** **LORD**. To prevent more sin, Saul used a large rock as a field altar so that the animals’ blood could be properly drained. The incident would never have occurred had it not been for Saul’s foolish oath.
**first of the altars:** This altar is the only one mentioned. David later built an altar that would become the site of God’s Temple ([2 Sam 24:18-25](2Sam.24.18-2Sam.24.25)).
**God made no reply:** Neither the “no” lot nor the “yes” lot of the Urim and Thummim appeared.

Casting **sacred lots** involved the Urim and Thummim ([Exod 28:30](Exod.28.30); [Lev 8:8](Lev.8.8)), which David also used when soliciting God’s guidance ([1 Sam 23:2](1Sam.23.2); [30:8](1Sam.30.8); [2 Sam 2:1](2Sam.2.1)). The Urim and Thummim were two small objects (perhaps flat stones, sticks, or arrows) that may have been cast like dice. They would provide a positive answer, a neutral response, or a negative answer.
**The people***,* aware of God’s blessing on the real hero of the day, were wiser than their king.

In contrast to the folly described in [14:1-46](1Sam.14.1-1Sam.14.46), these verses summarize Saul’s military successes. A similar summary of achievements ends the description of each king’s reign in 1 Samuel—2 Kings.
**secured his grasp:** Samuel had used this verb repeatedly when speaking about what a king would do: “He will take . . . take . . . take” ([8:10-18](1Sam.8.10-1Sam.8.18)).
**Moab, Ammon, Edom, . . . Zobah:** David confronted these same foes during his reign and expanded Israel’s territory in the process (see [2 Sam 8:1-14](2Sam.8.1-2Sam.8.14)).

**conquered the Amalekites:** See [15:1-35](1Sam.15.1-1Sam.15.35). The Amalekites, a nomadic group in the south, periodically raided and pillaged Israel (see [Exod 17:8-16](Exod.17.8-Exod.17.16); [Num 14:45](Num.14.45); [Judg 3:13](Judg.3.13); [6:3](Judg.6.3), [33](Judg.6.33); [7:12](Judg.7.12); [10:12](Judg.10.12)).
This information about Saul’s family, placed here rather than at the end of his reign, hints that his reign was essentially over and he would not be succeeded by one of his sons.
**Saul’s sons included:** Another of Saul’s sons was named Abinadab ([31:2](1Sam.31.2)).

**Ishbosheth** means “man of shame” (see study note on 2 Sam 2:8). He was also called Esh-baal (“man of Baal”). He served briefly as a rival king over the northern tribes during David’s early years ([2 Sam 2:8-11](2Sam.2.8-2Sam.2.11)).
**Ahinoam** is mentioned only here in Saul’s story. In [25:43](1Sam.25.43), David marries a woman also called Ahinoam (who might or might not have been the same person; cp. [2 Sam 12:8](2Sam.12.8)).

Saul had easily defeated the Ammonites ([11:11](1Sam.11.11)) but was having much less success with **the Philistines***,* given their well-organized fighting machine and their monopoly on iron and bronze ([13:19-22](1Sam.13.19-1Sam.13.22)).
**he drafted him:** Samuel had warned earlier that the king would take people as well as possessions ([8:11](1Sam.8.11)).
After Saul failed to obey God and completely destroy the Amalekites, God rejected him in even stronger terms than before (cp. [13:8-14](1Sam.13.8-1Sam.13.14)).
**LORD of Heaven’s Armies:** See study note on 1:3.

**to settle accounts:** In Moses’ time, **the nation of Amalek** had inhabited southern Judah and the Negev area south of Judah. As Israel traveled to Canaan, the Amalekites preyed on the sick and the weak and those traveling at the rear. They were the first people to attack Israel after the exodus from Egypt, for which God had promised to judge them ([Exod 17:8-16](Exod.17.8-Exod.17.16); [Deut 25:17-19](Deut.25.17-Deut.25.19)).
**completely destroy:** See “[Complete Dedication](themes:CompleteDedication)” Theme Note.
**Telaim:** Possibly Telem ([Josh 15:24](Josh.15.24)).
The unnamed town **in the valley** was located somewhere near a Negev *wadi,* a streambed or riverbed that fills with water only when rain falls.
**The Kenites** were nomadic metalworkers and descendants of Moses’ father-in-law ([Judg 1:16](Judg.1.16)).
**you showed kindness:** See [Exod 18](Exod.18.1-Exod.18.27); [Num 10:29-32](Num.10.29-Num.10.32).
The area where the Amalekites lived stretched **from Havilah** in northern Sinai **to Shur** near the eastern border **of Egypt**.
**Agag** was probably the descendant of an earlier king by the same name (see [Num 24:7](Num.24.7); cp. [Esth 3:1](Esth.3.1)).

**Saul and his men** directly disobeyed the Lord’s command to “completely destroy” the Amalekites ([15:3](1Sam.15.3)). Though the entire army participated in the disobedience of God’s command, Saul alone was responsible as their leader.
**Carmel** was a town near Hebron in southern Judah.
**Saul** commemorated his own accomplishments by erecting **a monument to himself**. In reality, he had earned shame ([15:16-19](1Sam.15.16-1Sam.15.19)).

**I have carried out the** **LORD’s command!** Cp. [15:3](1Sam.15.3). Saul apparently thought his actions were justified ([15:15](1Sam.15.15); cp. [Lev 22:19](Lev.22.19)). Samuel, however, cut through Saul’s pretense ([1 Sam 15:17-19](1Sam.15.17-1Sam.15.19)) and carried out God’s command himself ([15:32-33](1Sam.15.32-1Sam.15.33)).
Saul blamed **the army** even though he was the commander. Certainly, his real motivation was not spiritual ([15:9](1Sam.15.9)).
As the **anointed . . . king of Israel***,* Saul bore the responsibility for disobeying God, which neither false humility nor making excuses could diminish.
**my troops:** Saul persisted in blaming others (see [15:15](1Sam.15.15)).
**Gilgal** was a religious center. Saul tried to use religion to justify disobedience to God.
**What is more pleasing:** God values **obedience** much more than ritual (see also [Ps 40:6](Ps.40.6); [Hos 6:6](Hos.6.6); [Matt 12:7](Matt.12.7)).
**the fat of rams:** The choicest parts of the animal were offered to God.
**Rebellion . . . and stubbornness***,* sins of the heart, are as bad as the sinful practices of idolatrous pagans.
Scripture condemns **witchcraft** (see study note on Deut 18:10).
Saul finally confessed his sin. But it was too little, too late—and still accompanied by excuses.
**I was afraid of the people:** Saul continued to blame others (see [15:15](1Sam.15.15), [21](1Sam.15.21)).
**what they demanded:** There is no hint of such pressure in the chapter. Saul’s confession appears dishonest (cp. David, [2 Sam 12:13](2Sam.12.13); [Ps 51](Ps.51.1-Ps.51.19)).
Saul soon discovered who this **someone else** was ([18:8-9](1Sam.18.8-1Sam.18.9); cp. ch [16](1Sam.16.1-1Sam.16.23)).

**nor will he change his mind:** Samuel spoke prophetically of God’s commitment to make David king and to preserve his dynasty. God had rejected Saul, but he would never reject David (see [2 Sam 7:8-17](2Sam.7.8-2Sam.7.17)).
**honor me before the elders:** To help Saul save face.

The verb phrase **mourned constantly** is usually used for grieving over someone’s death. Although Saul was still living, his royalty was coming to an end. Samuel might have been grieving out of personal attachment to Saul, a sense of failure, or concern that Israel’s condition would be worse.
**the** **LORD was sorry:** See “[God’s Change of Mind](themes:GodsChangeOfMind)” Theme Note.

David was Saul’s replacement. There are striking similarities between the two: Samuel anointed both. Neither was pursuing the position. Both were unlikely candidates (Saul was from the smallest tribe; David was the youngest son). Both were impressive in appearance ([9:2](1Sam.9.2); [16:12](1Sam.16.12)). And the Spirit came mightily on each when he was anointed king ([10:10](1Sam.10.10); [11:6](1Sam.11.6); [16:13](1Sam.16.13)). The key difference was that David was “a man after \[God’s\] own heart” ([13:14](1Sam.13.14); cp. [16:7](1Sam.16.7)), while Saul was not.
**mourned long enough:** See study note on 15:35.
**Bethlehem** was about five miles south of Jerusalem. It was later known as the City of David ([Luke 2:11](Luke.2.11)) and the birthplace of Jesus.
**Jesse** was the grandson of Boaz and Ruth ([Ruth 4:22](Ruth.4.22)).

**I have selected:** This Hebrew verb implies that God had seen **one of \[Jesse’s\] sons** and based his choice on what he saw. God, the eternal king, knows better than the people of Israel how to choose a good **king** to serve the nation, and he provided a replacement for Saul who would lead Israel well.

**say that you have come to make a sacrifice:** God sometimes leads his servants into dangerous situations. He protects his own—sometimes by miracle, sometimes by strategy (cp. [Exod 3:18-22](Exod.3.18-Exod.3.22)). In Samuel’s role as a priestly judge, he would not have raised any suspicions by offering a sacrifice (see [1 Sam 10:8](1Sam.10.8)).
**the elders . . . came trembling:** News of Samuel’s rebuke of Saul and execution of Agag had likely reached Bethlehem.
**Purify yourselves:** Self-purification included bathing and abstaining from sexual intercourse (see [Exod 19:10-15](Exod.19.10-Exod.19.15); cp. [Gen 35:2-4](Gen.35.2-Gen.35.4)).
**The sacrifice** likely took place the following morning (see [Num 11:18](Num.11.18); [Josh 3:5](Josh.3.5); [7:13-14](Josh.7.13-Josh.7.14)).

**Samuel performed the purification rite for Jesse and his sons** to make sure they were ready for the sacrifice and for the anointing of the new king (cp. [Exod 19:10](Exod.19.10); [Josh 3:5](Josh.3.5)).

**his appearance or height:** Like Saul, **Eliab***,* Jesse’s oldest son, had an impressive outward appearance (cp. [9:2](1Sam.9.2)). Also like Saul, he was **rejected** (cp. [15:23](1Sam.15.23)). God had another man in mind to anoint as king.

**the** **LORD** **looks at the heart:** God can give a new heart ([10:9](1Sam.10.9)), touch hearts ([10:26](1Sam.10.26)), and peer into the deep motivations of the heart ([Ps 139:1](Ps.139.1)). God sees what people cannot see—a person’s true character. Eliab’s character comes out in [1 Sam 17:28](1Sam.17.28).

**The Spirit of the** **LORD came . . . upon David,** as was consistently evident (e.g., [16:23](1Sam.16.23); [17:48-54](1Sam.17.48-1Sam.17.54); [18:5](1Sam.18.5), [12-16](1Sam.18.12-1Sam.18.16)). The Spirit of the Lord had also come upon Saul ([10:10](1Sam.10.10)) but had left him because of disobedience ([16:14](1Sam.16.14)).
**Ramah:** Samuel’s hometown ([1:1](1Sam.1.1)).
Saul’s kingship continued its downward spiral after God’s Spirit departed from him. His reign ended in shame and defeat (ch [31](1Sam.31.1-1Sam.31.13)).
**Spirit . . . left Saul:** In contrast with David’s receiving the Spirit (see “[The Spirit’s Presence](themes:TheSpiritsPresence)” Theme Note).
**The** **LORD sent a tormenting spirit** as a consequence of Saul’s disobedience (see also [18:10](1Sam.18.10); [19:9](1Sam.19.9); cp. [Judg 9:23](Judg.9.23); [Rom 1:28-29](Rom.1.28-Rom.1.29)).
**harp:** The instrument was probably a lyre (as in [10:5](1Sam.10.5)).
**the** **LORD is with him:** People recognized that God’s Spirit was upon David ([16:13](1Sam.16.13)).
Although at first **Saul loved David very much***,* this love soon turned to intense jealousy and hatred (see [18:8-14](1Sam.18.8-1Sam.18.14)).

An **armor bearer** in ancient Israel served as the personal attendant of a warrior chieftain (see [14:1-15](1Sam.14.1-1Sam.14.15); [31:4-6](1Sam.31.4-1Sam.31.6); [Judg 9:54](Judg.9.54); [2 Sam 18:15](2Sam.18.15)).
David’s father, **Jesse** ([16:18](1Sam.16.18)), arranged for David to continue serving Saul while still fulfilling his shepherding duties at home (see [17:14-15](1Sam.17.14-1Sam.17.15)).

**Saul would feel better:** David was more than a handsome lad gifted in music; he was the anointed king. Here David illustrated what a king should be: one who brings relief. Later, David composed dozens of psalms that have brought comfort and relief through the ages.
**the tormenting spirit would go away:** Even those who are disobedient and rejected can receive relief and comfort through the Lord’s servant.
**The Philistines** presented an ongoing threat throughout Saul’s reign (see [14:47-52](1Sam.14.47-1Sam.14.52)).
**Socoh in Judah** was fourteen miles west of Bethlehem toward Philistine territory.
**Azekah** was a few miles northwest of Socoh (the precise location of **Ephes-dammim** is unknown). The Philistines were encroaching on Israelite territory.
The **valley of Elah** was a fertile area that ran east–west, fifteen miles southwest of Bethlehem.

**champion:** In ancient times, rival forces would sometimes agree to let selected individuals from each side decide a conflict. This reduced casualties and other costs. The same kind of combat is reflected in [2 Sam 2:12-17](2Sam.2.12-2Sam.2.17).
**Gath** was one of five Philistine cities with a reputation for having giants as citizens ([2 Sam 21:15-22](2Sam.21.15-2Sam.21.22)).
Although Goliath was a fully armored warrior of terrifying size, he did not have God—a far mightier warrior—on his side ([17:45-47](1Sam.17.45-1Sam.17.47)).
**Ephrathite:** Ephrath is a name for Bethlehem ([Gen 35:19](Gen.35.19); [1 Chr 4:4](1Chr.4.4)).

**went back and forth:** David apparently served as a musician and armor bearer in Saul’s court (see [16:19-23](1Sam.16.19-1Sam.16.23)) while maintaining his duties at home. The intermittent nature of David’s service might explain why Saul was unfamiliar with David during the encounter with Goliath (see [17:55-58](1Sam.17.55-1Sam.17.58)).

**What will a man get:** Cp. [18:17-27](1Sam.18.17-1Sam.18.27). David’s interest in a reward was overshadowed by his determination to silence Goliath’s defiance of God ([17:45-47](1Sam.17.45-1Sam.17.47)).
**pagan:** Literally *uncircumcised.* See study note on 14:6.
**Eliab . . . was angry***,* perhaps resentful that David, rather than he, was anointed to be king ([16:6-13](1Sam.16.6-1Sam.16.13)).
**I’ll go fight him!** David’s courage stands in contrast to Saul’s fear ([17:11](1Sam.17.11)).
A **stream** flowed through the valley of Elah ([17:2](1Sam.17.2)).

A **sling** was a leather pouch attached to two leather thongs. When the sling containing a stone was whirled rapidly, one of the thongs could be released, sending the stone toward its target. David probably became deadly accurate with a sling as a shepherd, but the sling was used by warriors as well ([Judg 20:16](Judg.20.16)).
**ruddy-faced:** The same Hebrew word is translated “dark” ([16:12](1Sam.16.12)) and “very red” ([Gen 25:25](Gen.25.25)). Here, it emphasizes David’s youthfulness and inexperience.
**boy:** Saul had expressed similar disbelief ([1 Sam 17:33](1Sam.17.33)). As a champion, Goliath expected to be met by an Israelite warrior of similar rank.
**a dog:** A metaphor for a compliant, bowing servant (cp. [2 Sam 9:8](2Sam.9.8)).
**a stick:** David had concealed his sling, and Goliath could see only his staff.

**by the names of his gods:** Since Goliath appealed to his gods, David’s victory over Goliath would also symbolize God’s victory over Dagon, the chief god of the Philistines ([1 Sam 5:2](1Sam.5.2), [5](1Sam.5.5)).
A corpse left to scavengers such as **birds and wild animals** was grievously cursed (cp. [Deut 21:23](Deut.21.23); [28:26](Deut.28.26)).
**the** **LORD of Heaven’s Armies:** See study note on 1:3. Despite the Philistines’ apparent military advantage, David knew that Israel had the supreme advantage in the one true God.
Goliath’s **forehead** remained exposed beneath his enormous helmet.
